definition: A word that sounds exactly like another word but has a different spelling and meaning, like their and there.
A short form that squeezes two words into one and marks the missing letters with an apostrophe, like they're for they are.
The little mark (') that shows missing letters in a contraction or shows that something belongs to someone.
A word or word form that shows who owns something, like their book or Maria's car.
Using two negative words in one statement, like I don't have no time, which cancels itself out or sounds nonstandard in formal English.
A saying whose meaning isn't clear from its words alone, like nip it in the bud, so changing a word breaks it.
Saying the same thing twice in one phrase, like free gift or past history, so one word is unnecessary.
A word that names a person, place, thing or idea, like teacher, kitchen or happiness.
One of the small words a, an or the that comes before a noun to show which one you mean.
A noun for things you can count one by one, like apple, car or idea, so you can say two apples or three cars.
A noun for something you measure instead of counting, like water, advice or traffic, so you can't put a number directly in front of it.
The form of a word that means just one, like dog or is.
The form of a word that means more than one, like dogs or are.
The comma placed before and or or at the end of a list of three or more things, like red, white, and blue.
A short form made from the first letters of a name or phrase, like DVD or NASA.
A group of words at the start of a sentence that sets the scene before the main point, like After lunch.
A joining word like and, but or so that links words, phrases or whole sentences.
A short word that stands in for a noun so you don't repeat it, like he, she, it, they or me.
The person or thing doing the action in a sentence: in Maria sings, Maria is the subject.
The person or thing receiving the action in a sentence: in Maria called Jake, Jake is the object.
A pronoun ending in self or selves, like myself or themselves, used when the doer and the receiver are the same person.
A word that describes a noun, like a quick lunch or a good idea.
A word that describes an action or another describing word, like quickly, well or very.
A word that shows an action or a state, like run, write, is or seem.
The rule that the verb must match its subject: one doer takes a singular verb, many doers take a plural verb.
A pronoun that points to no particular person or thing, like everyone, someone, nobody or each.
A noun that names a group as one unit, like team, family or committee.
The verb form that says something already happened, like walked or ate.
A verb whose past tense doesn't just add ed, like go and went or eat and ate.
The verb form used after have or has, like walked, eaten or gone.
A tense made with have or has plus a past participle, used for past events that still matter now, like I have finished.
Two full sentences jammed together with no proper joining word or punctuation between them.
Two full sentences joined by only a comma, which is not strong enough to hold them together.
A piece of a sentence punctuated as if it were whole, usually missing a subject or a verb.
A word or phrase that adds detail about another part of the sentence, like quickly or in the park.
A modifier sitting too far from the word it describes, so the sentence says something unintended.
